metaDescription: Bluetooth trackers and RF key finders under $25 compared by network, phone support, battery and loudness, with picks for iPhone, Android and no phone.
expertTake: The Apple AirTag 2nd generation is our top pick for iPhone owners, with the largest finding network and no subscription. The Qylara two pack is the value pick for iPhone users who want two Find My compatible tags. Anyone who wants a tracker that works away from home with an Android phone should skip the RF key finders, which only work within a short radio range.
introParagraphs: A Bluetooth tracker is a small tag that you attach to keys, a wallet or a bag. Your phone can ring it when it is nearby, and a crowd network of other phones can report where it was last seen when it is not.

Not every product sold as a key finder works that way. Simple RF finders use a handheld remote and have no phone, app or network. This guide ranks the true Bluetooth trackers first, then covers two RF finders as a different option. Prices move, and the $25 cap reflects listing prices when the guide was updated.

products.name: Apple AirTag 2nd generation, single tracker with Find My and Precision Finding

specList.label: Finding
specList.value: Precision Finding with step by step directions

specList.label: Speaker
specList.value: 50 percent louder than the first generation

products.description:
The second generation AirTag uses Apple's Find My network, which draws on a very large number of Apple devices to report location. It adds expanded Precision Finding on iPhone and Apple Watch, which shows step by step directions to the tag, and a speaker that is 50 percent louder than the original.

It works only with Apple devices, which is the main limit. An Android owner cannot set it up. For an iPhone household, the network size is the key advantage over every other tracker here, and there is no subscription for any feature. Compared with the Qylara pair, the AirTag offers Precision Finding and Apple's polish for the same cap but in a single tag. Compared with the Tile trackers, it has the larger network but no Android support.

Ownership is simple. The battery is a replaceable coin cell, and the app tells you when it is low. You need a holder or keyring accessory to attach it to keys, since the tag has no hole, and you should expect that to add to the total cost.
products.bestFor: iPhone owners who want the largest finding network with no subscription.
pros: Largest crowd finding network of any tracker here
Precision Finding gives step by step directions
Louder speaker is easier to hear in a bag or sofa
No subscription for any feature
cons: No keyring hole, so a holder is an extra purchase

products.name: Tile Pro Bluetooth tracker with SOS, works with iOS and Android

specList.label: App
specList.value: Free app, optional paid tier for some features

products.description:
The Tile Pro is the maker's most powerful tracker, and it works with both iPhone and Android, which no AirTag can. The free app lets you ring the tag, and a double press on the tag can ring your phone.

Its finding network draws on Tile and Life360 users, which is smaller than Apple's, so a lost item in a quiet area may take longer to report. Some features, such as smart alerts and location history, sit behind a paid tier, so check the current terms before you rely on them. Compared with the AirTag, it offers wider phone support but a smaller network. Compared with the Tile Slim, it is a keyring style tag with more range and a louder ring.

Ownership is about the tag battery. Check whether the listing says the battery is replaceable or sealed, because that decides whether you replace a cell or the whole tag. Keep the app updated and enable notifications for separation alerts.
products.bestFor: People who switch between iPhone and Android or share trackers across phones.
pros: Works with both iOS and Android phones
Loud ring and phone finder feature
SOS alert adds a safety use
Free app handles basic finding
cons: Smaller network than Apple Find My
Some features sit behind a paid tier

products.name: Qylara 2 pack Bluetooth tracker, works with Apple Find My, 80 to 100 dB buzzer
products.description:
The Qylara pack gives you two Find My compatible tags with a loud buzzer, replaceable CR2032 batteries and a water resistant design. The tags use the Apple Find My network, so they work with an iPhone and not an Android phone.

The 80 to 100 dB alarm is a maker claim, so judge it by how well you can hear the tag through a bag. Because it works through Find My, you get the large Apple network without the cost of an AirTag, though you lose Precision Finding and some polish in setup. Compared with the AirTag, you get two tags for the same cap but a less refined build. Compared with the Tile Slim, it offers a replaceable battery but no Android support.

Ownership requires a CR2032 battery change every year or so. Keep a spare, since a low battery tag can stop reporting. Test the buzzer at setup and then at a few months, and attach the tags with a keyring or a case.
products.bestFor: iPhone owners who want two tags for keys and a bag at a low cost.
pros: Two tags in one pack lower the cost per tag
Uses the large Apple Find My network
Replaceable CR2032 battery avoids waste
Water resistant design for daily carry
cons: iPhone only, with no Android support
Alarm figure is a maker claim and Precision Finding is absent

products.name: Tile Slim wallet finder Bluetooth tracker for wallets, passports and luggage tags

specList.label: Shape
specList.value: Card thin, fits a wallet slot

products.description:
The Tile Slim is a card shaped tracker that slides into a wallet, a passport holder or a luggage tag. The maker calls it its thinnest tracker, and it works with both iOS and Android.

A card shape solves the problem of attaching a tag to something with no keyring hole. The tradeoff is range and loudness, which are less than the keyring style Tile Pro, so it is better as a last known location tool than a find it by ear one. Compared with the AirTag, it fits a wallet without a holder. Compared with the Qylara tags, it works with Android but has a smaller network.

Ownership comes down to battery and tier. Check whether the battery is sealed, because a sealed battery means the tracker is replaced when it dies. As with the Pro, some features may require a paid tier, so confirm what you need is free.
products.bestFor: Wallets, passports and luggage tags where a card fits best.
pros: Card thin shape fits a wallet slot
Works with both iOS and Android
Tile app is free for basic ringing
Suited to luggage and passport holders
cons: Quieter and shorter range than keyring tags
Smaller network than Apple Find My

products.badge: Best RF Finder for No Phone
products.name: Reyke RF key finder with 131 ft range, 4 receivers and 1 transmitter
products.description:
The Reyke is not a Bluetooth tracker. It is an RF key finder with a handheld transmitter and four color coded receivers, and you press the matching button to make a receiver beep. There is no phone, no app and no network involved.

That makes it a very different tool. It works only within a short radio range, which the listing puts at 131 feet in open space, and walls cut that range sharply. It cannot show where something is when you are away from home, so it is a find it in the house tool and not a lost bag tool. Compared with the Esky, the Reyke has four receivers rather than six and a longer listed range. Compared with the AirTag, it needs no phone but cannot work at a distance.

Ownership is simple. The transmitter and each receiver use their own batteries, so keep spares, and test the beep at setup. It suits people who dislike phones, older users and anyone who mainly loses keys or remotes around the house.
products.bestFor: People who want a phone free finder for keys and remotes at home.
pros: No phone, app or account needed
Four color coded receivers for several items
Listed 131 foot range inside the home
Premium batteries included per the listing
cons: Different technology, only works near home
Walls and floors reduce the range

products.name: Esky RF key finder with 85 dB sound, LED light and 6 receivers

specList.label: Extras
specList.value: Stick on remote finder, wallet use

products.description:
The Esky is a radio frequency finder with six receivers, an 85 dB beep and an LED light on each tag. A stick on receiver can be attached to a TV remote, and the pack suits a household that loses several small items.

It is another phone free option, which means it shares the limits of the Reyke: range is about 100 feet listed and shorter through walls, and it only works near the transmitter. Six receivers give it the most items per set in the lineup. Compared with the Bluetooth trackers, it cannot show a last known location, and it needs a separate battery in each receiver. Compared with the Reyke, it has more receivers but a shorter listed range.

Ownership is about batteries and placement. Each receiver uses a small cell, so check them at set intervals, and keep the transmitter in a fixed spot such as a hook by the door. It suits families, caregivers and anyone who needs a simple, no setup finder.
products.bestFor: Households that lose several small items like remotes and keys indoors.
pros: Six receivers cover many items in one set
LED light helps in a dark room
No phone or app required
Stick on receiver suits a TV remote
cons: Different technology, short range near home only
Each receiver needs its own battery

buyingCriteria.explanation: A Bluetooth tracker depends on a crowd network of other phones. Apple Find My is the largest and works with iPhone only, Tile works with iPhone and Android but has a smaller network, and Android has its own network. Pick the one that matches your phone. The AirTag and Qylara use Find My, and the Tile models use the Tile network.

Bluetooth trackers report location through your phone and a crowd network. RF finders beep when you press a button on a remote and have no phone or network. They are not interchangeable. If you lose items away from home, buy a Bluetooth tracker. The Reyke and Esky are RF finders.

Replaceable coin cell batteries last about a year and cost little to swap, while sealed batteries last longer but mean replacing the tag. Check the listing for the battery type. Running out of battery silently stops a tracker from reporting. The AirTag and Qylara use replaceable batteries.

Ringing a tag helps when it is hidden nearby. Loud alarms matter for items in bags and sofas, and Bluetooth range matters for ringing from another room. Decibel figures on listings are maker claims. The Qylara claims 80 to 100 dB and the RF finders list 80 to 85 dB.
AirTag has no subscription. Tile has a free tier, with some features behind a paid tier. Check what you need is free. Features like location history and smart alerts are the usual paid items.

Keyring tags suit keys, and card shapes suit wallets. Some tags have no hole and need a holder. Choose a shape that fits where you will put it. The Tile Slim is a card, and the AirTag needs an accessory.

howWeEvaluated.title: Spec sheet review
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated network support, battery type, alarm loudness and form factor from each listing. We separated true Bluetooth trackers from RF finders. The AirTag and Tile Pro anchored the comparison.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for repeating comments about network coverage, battery life, loudness and setup. Those issues decide whether a tracker finds things. Network coverage in quiet areas came up most.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit for the phone and the item
howWeEvaluated.description: An iPhone owner, an Android owner and a person without a smartphone need different tools. We graded each product on that fit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cost relative to the cap
howWeEvaluated.description: Only listings at or below the $25 cap qualified, and we use relative tiers and quote no listing prices. The Qylara pack and RF sets sit at the low end.

howWeEvaluated.title: Claims we discounted
howWeEvaluated.description: Alarm volume and range claims vary widely between listings. We treat them as maker figures and rank on network and design.

maintenance.why: A low battery stops a tag from reporting. The app warns you, and a spare CR2032 solves it.
A silent tag is no help when you need it. Ring it from the app to confirm.
Network features rely on current software. Updates fix connection issues.
A worn clip drops the tag. Replace the accessory before it fails.
RF receivers and transmitters use small cells that run down quietly. Replace them before they fail.

faq.q: Do Bluetooth trackers work like GPS?
faq.a: No. They report a location only when a phone in the network passes within Bluetooth range. In remote areas, coverage can be thin.

faq.q: Will an AirTag work with Android?
faq.a: No. AirTags need an Apple device to set up and use. Tile trackers work with both iPhone and Android.

faq.q: Are RF key finders the same as Bluetooth trackers?
faq.a: No. RF finders use a handheld remote and short range radio, with no phone or network. They only help within about a hundred feet at home.

faq.q: Do I have to pay a subscription?
faq.a: AirTag needs none. Tile has a free tier, and some features such as location history may need a paid plan.

faq.q: Can a tracker be used to follow people?
faq.a: Phones alert you if an unknown tracker moves with you, and trackers should never be used to follow someone. Check your phone's safety alerts if you are concerned.

faq.q: How long do the batteries last?
faq.a: Coin cell trackers last about a year, and sealed ones can last longer. RF finders use small cells that need regular checking.
